title: The Man of Lawlessness and the Restrainer
summary: Paul urges the church not to be shaken by claims that the Day of the Lord has already come. First the rebellion must occur and the man of lawlessness be revealed, one who exalts himself above every god and sets himself in God's temple. Something now restrains him, but when he is revealed, deceiving those who refuse the truth, the Lord Jesus will destroy him at his coming. Paul thanks God for choosing the Thessalonians for salvation, urges them to hold to what they were taught, and prays for their comfort.
story: Chapter 1 assured the persecuted church that God would bring justice at the revelation of the Lord Jesus. Chapter 2 deals with the reason the letter was written: someone had told the Thessalonians that the Day of the Lord had already come, and they were alarmed. Paul does not respond with a date but with a sequence: the Day has not come, because certain things must happen first. He reminds them that he had taught them this in person (verse 5). The chapter then turns from the deception of those who are perishing to the security of those whom God has chosen, and closes with a prayer. It prepares for chapter 3, which turns from the future to daily life.
historical:
We do not know exactly what the Thessalonians had been told. Paul lists three possible sources: a spirit (a prophetic utterance), a message (a spoken report), or a letter seeming to be from us (verse 2). Some scholars think a forged letter in Paul's name had actually reached them; others think the church had misunderstood 1 Thessalonians. How anyone could believe the Day had already come is also unclear; perhaps they took the persecution as the beginning of the end, or held that the resurrection was already past in some spiritual sense (a view Paul later opposes in 2 Timothy 2:18).

The description of a ruler who exalts himself against God and sits in his temple had strong background in Jewish memory. Daniel 11:36 describes a king who exalts himself above every god, usually identified with the Seleucid king Antiochus IV Epiphanes, who in 167 BC set up a pagan altar in the Jerusalem temple, the abomination of desolation (Daniel 11:31; compare Mark 13:14). In AD 40, only about a decade before this letter, the emperor Gaius Caligula ordered his own statue set up in the Jerusalem temple; the order was delayed and then abandoned at his death in AD 41. Paul's first readers would have known that rulers could claim divine honors and threaten God's house.
cultural:
The Roman world was familiar with rulers who accepted worship. Emperors were honored with temples, priests, and sacrifices, especially in the Greek east, and some were proclaimed as gods after death or even during life. A figure who claimed to be God and demanded worship would not have seemed far-fetched.

The word parousia, used in verse 1 of Christ's coming, is used in verse 9 of the lawless one's coming, and the language of revelation is used of both as well (the noun apokalupsis of Christ in 1:7, the related verb of the lawless one in verses 3, 6, and 8), which sets up the lawless one as a counterfeit of Christ. The language of signs and wonders (verse 9) is the same used of genuine miracles, showing that miracles alone do not prove truth. The traditions of verse 15 were the teachings the apostles handed on, both in person and in writing; in the ancient world a teacher's school passed on its master's words carefully, and Paul asks the church to hold fast to what it received from him.
literary: The chapter has three parts. Verses 1 to 12 are a correction written in the style of apocalyptic, the kind of writing found in Daniel and Revelation that uses symbolic figures to speak of the end. It moves from the false claim (verses 1 and 2), to the events that must come first (verses 3 and 4), to a reminder of earlier teaching (verse 5), to the restrainer (verses 6 and 7), to the lawless one's revelation and destruction (verse 8), and to his deceptive work and its effect on those who refuse the truth (verses 9 to 12). Verses 13 and 14 are a thanksgiving that deliberately contrasts with what came before: against those who believe the lie, the believers are chosen, sanctified, and called through belief in the truth. Verses 15 to 17 give a command and a prayer. Because Paul writes as to people who already know what he means (you know what is now restraining him, verse 6), the passage is compressed and allusive, which is one reason it is so hard to interpret.

outline.t: Do not be shaken: the Day has not come
The rebellion and the man of lawlessness
The restrainer and the lawless one's defeat
Deception and the refusal of the truth
A prayer for comfort and strength

doctrines.note: Those who refuse the love of the truth and delight in wickedness are handed over to the lie they preferred (verses 10 to 12). God's judgment here takes the form of giving people what they have chosen, a pattern also seen in Romans 1:24-28.

Evil is real and active (the mystery of lawlessness is already at work), but it is restrained, revealed at the proper time, and destroyed by the Lord Jesus. Even the powerful delusion is sent by God (verse 11). Nothing in the story is outside his control.

God chose the believers from the beginning to be saved through the sanctifying work of the Spirit and belief in the truth, and called them through the gospel to share in Christ's glory (verses 13 and 14). Election here is a ground for thanksgiving and for standing firm.

words.note: Apostasia, rebellion or apostasy. In Greek the word could mean political revolt or religious defection. Here it names a great rebellion against God before the Day of the Lord. Interpreters differ on whether it refers mainly to a falling away within the church, a wider revolt of the world against God, or both. A few have argued that it means departure and refers to the rapture, but most scholars reject that sense.

Katecho, to hold back or restrain. Paul uses it first as a neuter participle, what is restraining (verse 6), and then as a masculine participle, the one who restrains (verse 7), so the restrainer seems to be both a force and a person. The Thessalonians knew what Paul meant; we do not, and Augustine admitted as much. The main suggestions are set out under the hard question below.

Aparche, firstfruits. In verse 13 the manuscripts divide: some read that God chose you from the beginning (ap' arches), which the Berean Standard Bible follows, while others read that God chose you as firstfruits (aparchen), which the underlying text used here has. The two differ by a single letter in Greek. Paul calls early converts firstfruits elsewhere (Romans 16:5; 1 Corinthians 16:15), which supports one reading; from the beginning emphasizes God's eternal choice, which supports the other.

christ: Against the lawless one, who exalts himself and claims to be God, stands the Lord Jesus, who will destroy him with the breath of his mouth and by the majesty of his arrival (verse 8). The phrase echoes Isaiah 11:4, where the Spirit-filled king from the line of David slays the wicked with the breath of his lips. The lawless one is a counterfeit: he has his own coming, his own revelation, and his own signs, but his claims are a lie, and a single breath from the true Lord ends him. The contrast is also moral. The lawless one grasps at divinity; Christ, as Philippians 2 says, did not grasp at equality with God but humbled himself. Believers are called to share in the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ (verse 14), and the chapter's prayer names him first, before God our Father, as the source of eternal comfort and good hope (verse 16).

hard.q: Who is the man of lawlessness, and who or what is the restrainer?
hard.a: Paul says the Thessalonians knew; later readers have had to guess, and faithful Christians have landed in different places. On the man of lawlessness, the main readings are these. Futurist interpreters, following early writers such as Irenaeus, see a single individual who will arise shortly before Christ's return, the Antichrist of Christian tradition, and some expect a rebuilt temple in Jerusalem. Preterist interpreters look to Paul's own century: the memory of Caligula's statue, the emperor Nero, or the rebel leaders and Roman armies of the war that ended with the temple's destruction in AD 70. Historicist interpreters, including many Reformers and the original Westminster Confession of 1646, identified the man of sin with the papacy claiming authority in the church, God's temple; few hold this view today, and Catholic readers have naturally rejected it. Idealist interpreters see a recurring pattern of human rebellion against God, embodied again and again in rulers and systems, which will reach a final climax. On the restrainer, suggestions include the Roman Empire and its rule of law (a view found as early as Tertullian), the Holy Spirit or the Spirit working through the church (common among pretribulation readers, who connect his removal with the rapture), the preaching of the gospel to the nations, the archangel Michael, or God himself. Each reading can point to features of the text; none has settled the question. Paul's own purpose is clear on any reading: the Day has not yet come, evil is held in check, and the Lord Jesus will defeat it.

questions: Paul responds to alarming end-times claims by pointing the church back to what it had been taught. How should Christians respond to confident predictions about the end today?
The lawless one deceives those who refuse the love of the truth. What does it mean to love the truth, and not only to know it?
How does knowing that God chose and called you (verses 13 and 14) help you stand firm when you are unsettled?
